content: The health effects resulting from the September 11, 2001, attacks have raised significant concerns, particularly for those in the Financial District of Lower Manhattan. The collapse of the Twin Towers and Building 7 of the World Trade Center released a massive cloud of pulverized building materials, electronic equipment, and furniture into the surrounding area. This toxic dust continued to linger in the air for months after the attacks, exposing residents, workers, and first responders to hazardous substances. The dust from the collapsed towers was described as wildly toxic by air pollution expert Dr. Thomas Cahill. It contained 8% asbestos, as well as lead, mercury, crystalline silica, cadmium, and polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs), many of which are carcinogenic. Fires at the site burned for three months, releasing unprecedented levels of dioxins and other harmful chemicals. These substances have been linked to respiratory illnesses, kidney damage, heart disease, liver dysfunction, and nervous system deterioration. First responders and recovery workers have experienced debilitating illnesses, including pulmonary fibrosis, which led to the death of NYPD member Cesar Borja. Many first responders have developed severe respiratory ailments, and health effects have also been reported among residents, students, and office workers in Lower Manhattan and nearby Chinatown. In November 2006, it was reported that several dozen recovery workers had developed cancers, including blood cell cancers, which top doctors and epidemiologists have linked to exposure to toxins at Ground Zero. Dr. Larry Norton of Memorial Sloan-Kettering Hospital highlighted the 70% illness rate among first responders as a wake-up call and questioned why the nation was not mobilizing to address the chronic health impacts of the disaster. Other experts, including environmental health professors and epidemiologists, have argued that the cancer cases among monitored individuals are not coincidental and are likely caused by the toxic Ground Zero cloud. The American College of Preventive Medicine has expressed concern about the potential development of malignant mesothelioma among those exposed to Ground Zero air. Ongoing studies, such as those conducted by Columbia University and Mount Sinai Medical Center, are monitoring the health of first responders, residents, and children exposed to the toxic environment. These studies aim to assess the long-term health effects and developmental impacts on children whose mothers were pregnant during the attacks. A 2006 study of firefighters revealed that those who inhaled Ground Zero air lost approximately 12 years of lung function. Similarly, a Mount Sinai report found that 70% of recovery and rescue workers experienced a decline in respiratory function between 2002 and 2004. Despite these findings, 40% of World Trade Center workers monitored by Mount Sinai lacked health insurance, complicating their access to necessary medical care. The deadline for Ground Zero-related workers' compensation claims was extended to August 2008 by Governor Eliot Spitzer, allowing more individuals to register for benefits. However, fewer than 14,000 of the estimated 100,000 eligible individuals had registered by the initial deadline in 2007. Mayor Michael Bloomberg appointed Jeffrey Hon as the World Trade Center health coordinator in 2007 to address inconsistencies in city agency responses and to manage health-related issues. However, conflicting statements about Hon's role have raised questions about the effectiveness of the city's efforts. Early warnings about the health risks were muted. On September 12, 2001, federal scientist Dr. Edwin Kilbourne cautioned against a rapid return to buildings near Ground Zero due to potential hazards from toxic materials. However, safety protocols for workers at the site were not adequately enforced, as noted by Associate City Health Commissioner Kelly McKinney. Political controversies have also emerged. President George W. Bush and then-Mayor Rudy Giuliani have been criticized for allegedly minimizing health risks and rushing to reopen the Financial District to maintain economic stability. Former EPA Administrator Christine Todd Whitman assured the public that the air was safe to breathe, but an August 2003 report by the EPA's Office of the Inspector General revealed that the Bush administration pressured the agency to downplay health risks. Key warnings about asbestos and other toxins were altered or removed from public statements. Numerous lawsuits have been filed against the City of New York for failing to provide proper protective equipment to cleanup workers. In 2006, a federal judge rejected the city's motion to dismiss lawsuits seeking health payments for first responders. By 2007, the monthly cost of treating Ground Zero workers had risen to $20 million, reflecting the increasing number of sick workers and the worsening severity of their illnesses. The health impacts have been devastating for many individuals. First responders, such as NYPD Detective James Zadroga, were among the first to have their deaths directly linked to toxic exposure at Ground Zero. Other responders, including Cesar Borja, Robert Williamson, Kevin Hawkins, and Frank Macri, succumbed to cancers and respiratory diseases believed to be caused by their work at the site. Volunteers, janitorial workers, and office personnel have also suffered from illnesses related to the toxic environment. Students and staff at nearby schools, such as Stuyvesant High School, returned to their buildings while fires were still burning at Ground Zero. Alumni have since called for greater attention to health problems related to the toxic air, and debates continue over whether cases of cancer among students and staff are linked to their exposure. The long-term health consequences of the September 11 attacks remain a critical issue, with ongoing monitoring and research needed to fully understand the impact on those exposed to the toxic environment.
